chapters.title: Part I: Nature and Significance of Management

topics.title: Management: getting things done effectively and efficiently

learn.hook: A Mumbai dabbawala team delivers lakhs of lunch boxes on time, at very low cost, using simple coding. That is management at work: right result, least waste.
points: Management is the process of getting things done, with the aim of achieving goals effectively and efficiently, through and with other people.
It is a process: a series of linked functions (planning, organising, staffing, directing, controlling).
Effectiveness means doing the right task and completing it on time, that is, achieving the goal.
Efficiency means doing the task correctly with minimum cost, that is, the best use of resources (input vs output).
Both matter: a manager should aim for high effectiveness AND high efficiency. Finishing on time at a huge cost, or saving cost but missing the deadline, is poor management.

example.q: A firm must make 10,000 school bags by 30 June. It finishes on 25 June, but wastage of cloth pushes cost 20% above budget. Is the firm effective, efficient, both or neither?
steps: Effectiveness asks: was the goal achieved on time? Yes, the bags were ready before 30 June.
Efficiency asks: were resources used at minimum cost? No, cost overshot because of wastage.
So the firm was effective but not efficient.

learn.reallife: ISRO is admired for both: its Mars Orbiter Mission reached Mars on its first attempt (effective) at a famously low budget (efficient).

quiz.explain: Efficiency compares output with input; it is about cost and resources.

quiz.explain: The goal was met on time (effective), but extra cost means resources were not used optimally (not efficient).

Because it is a series of interrelated functions performed by all managers
Because it is done only by the CEO
Because it is a written rulebook
quiz.explain: Planning, organising, staffing, directing and controlling are linked functions that together make up the management process.

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Effectiveness and efficiency always go together. Reason (R): A task can be finished on time even if more resources are used than needed.

Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A

quiz.explain: The goal (winning) was met and resources stayed within the planned cost, so both conditions hold.
quiz.mistake: Thinks spending the full budget is always inefficient

teach.ask: Gappu is puzzled: 'If my nest is built on time, isn't that enough? Why do people keep saying efficient AND effective?'
teach.praise: Tweet! So effective means reaching the goal on time, and efficient means not wasting resources. I need both for a good nest!
teach.nudge: You told me about finishing on time. What about the cost or the twigs I use? Is there a second idea?

learn.hook: A temple trust, a hospital, a startup and a gram panchayat all look different, yet each needs management. What makes management the same everywhere?
points: Goal-oriented process: every management activity is aimed at achieving set goals.
All-pervasive: needed in all organisations (business, school, hospital, government), at all levels and in all countries.
Multidimensional: it covers management of work, management of people (as individuals and groups) and management of operations.
Continuous: functions are performed again and again; it never stops. Group activity: it works through people with different needs towards common goals.
Dynamic function: it adapts to the changing environment. Intangible force: it cannot be seen, but its presence is felt in order, results and employee satisfaction.

example.q: A visitor to Sharma Electronics notices that targets are met, staff are cheerful and work flows smoothly, though nobody can 'point to' management. Which characteristic is shown?
steps: The visitor cannot see management directly.
Its effect is felt through results and a smooth work environment.
This is the intangible nature of management.

learn.reallife: When a smartphone brand in India shifted to selling online during the 2020 lockdown, it showed management as a dynamic function that adapts to change.

teach.praise: Wonderful! Goal-oriented, everywhere, non-stop, adaptable and invisible but felt. Now I see it in my own flock!

learn.hook: A company can earn crores and still fail if it pollutes the river next door or treats its staff badly. Good management juggles three sets of goals.
points: Organisational objectives: survival (earn enough to cover costs), profit (cover costs and risks, reward owners) and growth (sales, employees, products, capital).
Social objectives: creating benefit for society, e.g. using environment-friendly methods, giving employment to disadvantaged sections, providing basic amenities like schools and creches.
Personal objectives: satisfying employees' needs: financial (competitive salary), social (recognition by peers) and higher-level needs (personal growth and development).
Importance: achieving group goals, increasing efficiency, creating a dynamic organisation (helps people adapt to change), achieving personal objectives, and helping in the development of society.

example.q: Green Leaf Paper Mill installs a water-recycling plant and runs a free school for workers' children. Which objective is it pursuing?
steps: The actions do not directly raise profit or employee pay.
They benefit the environment and the community.
So they fall under social objectives.

learn.reallife: Many Indian companies run schools, health camps and water projects near their plants under CSR, a clear example of the social objective of management.

topics.title: Management as an art, a science and a profession

learn.hook: Two managers read the same textbook, yet one turns a struggling shop around and the other doesn't. Is management a science, an art, or both?
points: Art (features met): existence of theoretical knowledge, personalised application (each manager applies it in her own style) and based on practice and creativity.

Science: a systematised body of knowledge, principles based on experimentation and observation, and universal validity. Management has the first two, but its principles are not exactly universal because it deals with people, so it is an inexact (soft or behavioural) science.
Profession features: well-defined body of knowledge, restricted entry (by an exam or degree), professional association, ethical code of conduct and service motive.

Management meets only some: it has a well-defined body of knowledge, but there is no restricted entry (no degree is legally required to become a manager), membership of associations like AIMA is not compulsory, and its code of conduct is not binding.
Conclusion: management has the features of an art, of an (inexact) science and some features of a profession.

example.q: Why can't management be called a full profession like law or chartered accountancy?
steps: A lawyer must be enrolled with the Bar Council and a CA must be a member of ICAI: entry is restricted.
Anyone can be appointed a manager; an MBA is desirable but not legally required.
Membership of a managers' association is voluntary and its code of conduct is not binding.
So management fails the tests of restricted entry, compulsory professional association and a binding ethical code.
example.answer: It lacks restricted entry, a compulsory professional body and a binding code of conduct

learn.reallife: An Indian cricket captain uses the same tactics theory as everyone, but places fielders in a personal style. Like management, captaincy is both a science and an art.

games.title: Art, science or profession feature?

games.title: Is management a profession?
items: Management has a well-defined body of knowledge.
It is taught in colleges and has a large literature.
A person must hold an MBA to be legally appointed as a manager.
No degree is legally required; there is no restricted entry.
Membership of a managers' association is compulsory in India.
Associations like AIMA exist, but membership is voluntary.

quiz.q: Management is called an inexact science because:
options: It has no body of knowledge
It deals with human behaviour, so its principles must be modified to suit situations
It is practised only by scientists
quiz.explain: Principles exist and are tested, but people behave differently, so results are not exact.
quiz.mistake: Thinks management has no principles at all

quiz.q: Which feature of art does management satisfy when two managers apply the same principles in different styles?
quiz.explain: Applying the same knowledge in one's own style is personalised application, a feature of art.
quiz.mistake: Picks a feature of science or profession

quiz.q: Which feature of a profession does management clearly satisfy?
quiz.explain: Management knowledge is well defined and taught; the other features are not fully met.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the existence of AIMA makes membership compulsory

quiz.q: Anyone can be appointed a manager irrespective of qualification. Which feature of a profession does management NOT meet?
quiz.explain: A profession restricts entry through an exam or degree; management does not.
quiz.mistake: Confuses features of art and science with those of a profession

quiz.q: 'Principles of management are developed after repeated observation and testing in different organisations.' This shows management as a:
quiz.explain: Principles based on experimentation and observation are a feature of science.
quiz.mistake: Thinks practice-based learning means art only

quiz.q: What is the correct conclusion about the nature of management?
options: It is a pure science like chemistry
It is a full profession like law
It has features of an art and an inexact science, and some features of a profession
quiz.explain: Management meets all features of art, most of science (inexact) and only some of a profession.

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Management is a full-fledged profession. Reason (R): Management has a well-defined body of knowledge.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is false because management lacks restricted entry and a binding code. R is true but having knowledge alone does not make it a profession.
quiz.mistake: Thinks one profession feature is enough to call it a profession

quiz.q: Manager Nisha keeps improving her handling of team conflicts through years of practice and fresh ideas. This reflects which feature of art?
quiz.explain: Art improves with practice and creative use of knowledge.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up features of art and science

teach.ask: Gappu wonders: 'My mama says management is a science, my papa says it's an art. Who wins?'
teach.praise: Ha! Both win, and the profession part is only partly true. Mama and papa can stop arguing now!
teach.nudge: You've told me one side. Is it also a science, or a profession? What's missing?

learn.hook: In a large company, who decides to enter a new country, who sets the sales team's monthly duties, and who makes sure the machine operators wear helmets? Three different levels!
points: Levels show the hierarchy of superior-subordinate (authority-responsibility) relationships: top, middle and supervisory (operational).

Top management (chairman, CEO, MD, chief operating officer, president, vice-presidents, board): integrates diverse elements, sets overall goals, strategies and policies, and is responsible for the welfare and survival of the organisation. It analyses the business environment.

Middle management (division or department heads, plant superintendents, operations managers): interprets the policies framed by top management, ensures the department has the necessary personnel, assigns duties, motivates staff and cooperates with other departments. It is the link between top and supervisory levels.

Supervisory or operational management (foremen, supervisors): directly oversees workers, ensures quality of output, minimises wastage, maintains safety standards and passes on workers' problems to higher levels. It links management with the workforce.

example.q: Identify the level: (i) deciding to set up a plant in Odisha; (ii) assigning sales targets to each regional team; (iii) checking that workers on the shop floor follow safety rules.
steps: (i) is a long-term strategic decision, so top management.
(ii) interprets policy and assigns duties, so middle management.
(iii) directly oversees workers, so supervisory management.

learn.reallife: In a large Indian bank, the board and managing director set strategy (top), zonal and regional heads turn it into targets for branches (middle), and branch-level officers supervise daily counter work (supervisory).

teach.ask: Gappu is confused: 'In a big company, isn't everyone just a manager? Why talk about levels?'
teach.praise: Tweet! Top sets the direction, middle turns it into plans, supervisors make it happen on the floor.
teach.nudge: Good! Can you tell me what each of the three levels actually does?

learn.hook: Organising a school annual day? You decide what to do, form teams, pick people, guide them, and check if all is on track. You just did all five management functions!
points: Planning: deciding in advance what to do and how to do it. It bridges where we are and where we want to be.
Organising: assigning tasks, grouping them into departments, allocating resources and setting authority relationships.
Staffing: finding and keeping the right people in the right jobs (recruitment, selection, training).
Directing: leading, influencing, motivating and communicating with employees to perform tasks.
Controlling: monitoring performance, comparing it with standards and taking corrective action. The usual sequence is planning, organising, staffing, directing, controlling.

example.q: A shop owner (i) decides to open a second branch by Diwali, (ii) divides work among three teams, (iii) hires two cashiers, (iv) motivates staff with a festive bonus, (v) checks weekly sales against targets. Name each function.
steps: (i) Deciding in advance = planning
(ii) Dividing work = organising
(iii) Hiring = staffing
(iv) Motivating = directing
(v) Comparing with targets = controlling

learn.reallife: Before a big IPL season, a franchise plans its strategy, organises support staff, picks players at the auction (staffing), the captain leads them (directing) and analysts track performance (controlling).

learn.hook: An orchestra has brilliant musicians, but without the conductor it is noise. In business, that conductor is coordination.
points: Coordination is the process by which a manager synchronises the activities of different departments so that group efforts move towards common goals. It is the force that binds all the other functions.

Characteristics: integrates group efforts, ensures unity of action, is a continuous process, is all-pervasive, is the responsibility of all managers and is a deliberate function (it does not happen on its own).

Importance: growth in size (more people and units to link), functional differentiation (departments may pull in different directions) and specialisation (specialists often think only of their own area).
Coordination is called the essence of management because it is needed at all levels (top, middle, supervisory) and in all functions (planning to controlling). It is not a separate function.

example.q: At Zenith Appliances, production made 50,000 fans but marketing had orders for only 30,000. Which management element was missing, and why does it matter?
steps: Each department worked hard but pursued its own target.
There was no matching of production with sales.
Coordination would have synchronised the two departments towards a common goal, avoiding unsold stock.
example.answer: Coordination; it integrates departmental efforts towards common goals

learn.reallife: At the Kumbh Mela, railways, police, health services and local bodies must work in step. That synchronisation of many departments is coordination on a giant scale.

A function of top management only
The force that binds all the other functions of management
An automatic result of good planning
quiz.explain: Coordination runs through all functions and binds them together.

quiz.q: Why is coordination called the essence of management?

Because it is the last function

quiz.q: The finance department wants to cut costs while the marketing department wants a bigger advertising budget. Which reason for coordination is shown?
quiz.explain: Separate departments may pursue their own objectives, so coordination is needed.

quiz.q: Specialists such as IT experts and lawyers often believe only they know how their work should be done. This creates a need for coordination due to:
quiz.explain: Specialists focus on their own field and must be integrated with others.

quiz.q: Assertion (A): Coordination is the responsibility of all managers. Reason (R): Coordination is needed only at the top level, where overall policies are made.
options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: A is true: managers at every level coordinate. R is false because coordination is needed at all levels, not just the top.
quiz.mistake: Thinks coordination is only a top management task

quiz.q: Which is NOT a characteristic of coordination?
quiz.explain: Coordination is continuous, not a one-time activity.

teach.praise: Aha! Hard work alone isn't enough; someone must deliberately line everyone up. Coordination is the essence!
teach.nudge: Close! Can you say why it's called the essence of management, or why it doesn't happen on its own?

topics.title: Principles of management: meaning and nature

learn.hook: Traffic rules tell you exactly what to do. Management principles are different: they are flexible guidelines that bend to fit each situation.
points: A principle of management is a broad and general guideline for decision-making and behaviour of managers.
Principles are not techniques: techniques are procedures or methods (a series of steps), while principles guide the choices a manager makes while using techniques.
Principles are not values: values are general rules of behaviour accepted by society, while principles are technical guidelines for managerial action.

Nature: universal applicability, general guidelines, formed by practice and experimentation, flexible, mainly behavioural, show cause-and-effect relationships, and contingent (application depends on the situation).

example.q: A manager applies 'division of work' strictly in a car factory but only partly in a small design studio. Which feature of principles does this show?
steps: The same principle is used in both places.
It is modified to suit the size and nature of each firm.
Principles can be adapted, so they are flexible (and contingent on the situation).

learn.reallife: A cricket coach's principle 'keep the batting order stable' is a guideline, not a law. In a tight chase the order may change. Management principles work the same way.

quiz.explain: Principles apply in all organisations, but not in exactly the same way, because their application depends on the situation. So A is false and R is true.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the words 'in exactly the same way'

teach.praise: So principles guide but bend to fit the situation. Not rigid rules, but not to be ignored either!
teach.nudge: Okay, but what kind of thing is a principle, and can it be changed for a situation?

learn.hook: Why do companies spend lakhs training managers in principles when anyone can learn by trial and error? Because trial and error is expensive!
points: Provide managers with useful insights into reality: they improve knowledge, ability and understanding of managerial situations.
Optimum utilisation of resources and effective administration: they help avoid wastage and limit personal bias in administration.

Scientific decisions: decisions become thoughtful, justifiable and free from bias. Meeting changing environment requirements: e.g. division of work leads to specialisation, which suits changing technology.
Fulfilling social responsibility: e.g. fair remuneration and equity. Management training, education and research: principles form the base of management courses and new techniques.

example.q: Why does an MBA course begin with principles of management rather than straight case studies?
steps: Principles form the core knowledge of management.
They are the base for training, education and research.
Without principles, learners cannot analyse cases logically.
example.answer: Because principles are the basis of management training, education and research

learn.reallife: Large Indian companies run 'management trainee' programmes that start with core management principles, showing their role in training and education.

options: Optimum utilisation of resources and effective administration

options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A

quiz.explain: Knowing likely effects helps managers choose actions that avoid waste, so R explains A.

teach.praise: Got it! Principles save time, money and bias. Trial and error is the expensive way!
teach.nudge: Figuring it out costs something. What do principles save, and where else are they useful?

learn.hook: In the 1880s an American engineer stood with a stopwatch on a factory floor and asked: 'Is there ONE best way to do this job?' His name was F.W. Taylor.
points: F.W. Taylor (1856-1915) is called the father of scientific management. He defined it as knowing exactly what you want people to do and seeing that they do it in the best and cheapest way.
Science, not rule of thumb: replace guesswork and trial and error with scientific study of work to find the one best way.
Harmony, not discord: management and workers should understand each other; this needs a complete 'mental revolution' on both sides.
Cooperation, not individualism: cooperation between workers and management replaces competition; management should reward workers' suggestions and workers should not strike unreasonably.
Development of each and every person to his or her greatest efficiency and prosperity: scientific selection and training of workers so each reaches full efficiency.

example.q: At Meghna Steel, managers and workers used to blame each other. Now management shares productivity gains and workers suggest better methods. Which principle is this?
steps: The change is in the attitude of both sides.
They now see each other as partners, not rivals.
Such a change of mindset is the mental revolution behind 'harmony, not discord'.

learn.reallife: Many Indian factories run 'suggestion schemes' that reward workers for ideas that save cost, an example of Taylor's 'cooperation, not individualism'.

teach.praise: Wow! Science over guesswork, harmony, cooperation and growing every worker. No wonder he's called the father of scientific management!

topics.title: Taylor's techniques: functional foremanship and standardisation

learn.hook: Imagine eight bosses for one worker, each an expert in one thing! Taylor actually proposed this to make factories better.
points: Functional foremanship: separation of planning from execution (doing). It extends division of work and specialisation to the shop floor. Each worker gets orders from eight specialist foremen.

Under the planning in-charge: instruction card clerk (drafts instructions for workers), route clerk (specifies the route or sequence of production), time and cost clerk (prepares time and cost sheets) and disciplinarian (ensures discipline).

Under the production in-charge: speed boss (timely and accurate completion of jobs), gang boss (keeps machines and tools ready for work), repair boss (keeps machines in proper working condition) and inspector (checks quality of work).
Standardisation of work: setting standards for every business activity, such as process, raw material, time, product, machinery, methods and working conditions.
Simplification of work: eliminating unnecessary diversity of products, i.e. needless varieties, sizes and dimensions. It saves cost of labour, machines and tools, and reduces inventory.

example.q: A factory makes a bucket in 22 sizes, but 90% of sales come from 5 sizes. Which technique should it use and what is the benefit?
steps: Many sizes mean extra moulds, inventory and labour.
Dropping the unnecessary varieties is simplification.
Benefit: lower costs, fuller use of machines and less inventory.

learn.reallife: The Bureau of Indian Standards sets standards for products like helmets and cement, which echoes Taylor's idea of standardisation.

quiz.q: Functional foremanship is based on the separation of:
quiz.explain: Taylor separated planning and doing, with specialists for each.

quiz.q: How many specialist foremen does a worker report to under functional foremanship?
quiz.explain: Four under the planning in-charge and four under the production in-charge make eight.

quiz.q: Which foreman is responsible for keeping machines and tools ready for operation?
quiz.explain: The gang boss keeps machines and tools ready; the repair boss maintains their working condition.
quiz.mistake: Confuses gang boss with repair boss

quiz.q: Which of these works under the planning in-charge?
quiz.explain: Planning in-charge: instruction card clerk, route clerk, time and cost clerk, disciplinarian.

quiz.q: Functional foremanship violates which principle of Fayol?
quiz.explain: One worker gets orders from eight bosses, which goes against having one boss.
quiz.mistake: Thinks it violates division of work, which it actually extends

quiz.q: Eliminating unnecessary varieties, sizes and dimensions of a product is called:
quiz.explain: Simplification removes needless diversity; standardisation sets benchmarks.

quiz.explain: Setting standards for processes, materials and methods is standardisation.

options: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true, but R is false
A is false, but R is true
quiz.explain: Because each foreman handles one specialised function, it extends division of work to the shop floor.
quiz.mistake: Thinks functional foremanship works against specialisation

teach.ask: Gappu gasps: 'Eight bosses?! Why would Taylor want that?'
teach.praise: Eight specialists, each doing one job well, with planning separated from doing. Clever, though confusing for the worker!
teach.nudge: Think about planning and doing. What did Taylor separate, and why have specialists?

topics.title: Work study and the differential piece wage system

learn.hook: A worker loading bricks bends 40 times an hour. Could the same output come with 25 bends and less tiredness? Taylor's work-study techniques ask exactly that.
points: Method study: finding the one best way of doing a job, from procuring raw material to delivering the product, to cut cost and raise quality.
Motion study: studying the movements of a worker or machine to eliminate unnecessary motions.
Time study: fixing the standard time to complete a well-defined job. It helps decide the number of workers, frame incentive schemes and estimate labour costs.
Fatigue study: deciding the amount and frequency of rest intervals so workers can regain stamina.
Differential piece wage system: two piece rates, a higher rate for workers who reach or exceed the standard output and a lower rate for those below it. Wage = units produced x applicable rate.

example.q: Standard output is 10 units a day. Rate: ₹50 per unit at or above standard, ₹40 per unit below standard. Asha makes 12 units and Bala makes 8. Find their wages and the difference.
steps: Asha reaches the standard: 12 x ₹50 = ₹600
Bala is below the standard: 8 x ₹40 = ₹320
Difference = ₹600 - ₹320 = ₹280

learn.reallife: Delivery apps that pay riders more per order after a daily target is crossed use the same idea as Taylor's differential piece wage system.

topics.title: Fayol's principles (1): division of work to remuneration

learn.hook: Henri Fayol ran a French mining company for 30 years and turned his experience into 14 principles still asked in every board exam.
points: Henri Fayol (1841-1925) is the father of general management. He gave 14 principles based on his personal experience.

Division of work: work is divided into small tasks, each done by a trained specialist. Authority and responsibility: there must be a balance (parity) between the two. Discipline: obedience to rules; needs good superiors at all levels, clear and fair agreements and judicious penalties.
Unity of command: an employee should get orders from only one superior. Its violation undermines authority, threatens discipline and creates confusion.

Unity of direction: one head and one plan for each group of activities with the same objective. Unity of command concerns a single employee; unity of direction concerns the whole organisation (or a division).

Subordination of individual interest to general interest: the organisation's interest comes first. Remuneration of employees: pay should be fair and just, allowing a reasonable standard of living within the company's paying capacity.

example.q: At Nova Foods, a packing worker gets one order from the production manager and an opposite order from the marketing manager. Which principle is violated and what is the effect?
steps: The worker has two bosses giving conflicting orders.
One employee should receive orders from only one superior.
Effect: confusion, weak authority and poor discipline.
example.answer: Unity of command is violated, causing confusion

learn.reallife: Indian Railways has separate zones, each with its own General Manager and plans for its region, an example of unity of direction.

topics.title: Fayol's principles (2): centralisation to esprit de corps

learn.hook: Two managers at the same level in different departments need to talk urgently, but the formal route goes all the way up and down. Fayol had a shortcut: the gang plank.
points: Centralisation and decentralisation: a balance is needed between concentrating decisions at the top and spreading them to lower levels.

Scalar chain: the formal line of authority from the highest to the lowest rank, which communication should follow. Gang plank: in an emergency, employees at the same level (e.g. E and O) may contact each other directly.

Order: 'a place for everything and everyone, and everything and everyone in its place' (material and human order). Equity: kindliness and justice; no discrimination on the basis of caste, religion, sex, language, nationality or other such grounds.
Stability of personnel: employees, once selected and trained, should be kept in their posts long enough to show results; frequent turnover is costly.
Initiative: workers should be encouraged to develop and carry out their plans (e.g. a suggestion system). Esprit de corps: team spirit and unity; the manager should replace 'I' with 'We'.

example.q: A firm hires and fires sales staff every three months. Which principle is violated and what is a likely consequence?
steps: Employees are not kept long enough to settle and perform.
This goes against stability of personnel.
Consequence: high hiring and training costs, low efficiency and insecurity.
example.answer: Stability of personnel; higher costs and lower efficiency

learn.reallife: Indian cricket's famous team huddles and 'we win together' talk reflect esprit de corps: union is strength.

topics.title: Fayol versus Taylor and case applications

learn.hook: Fayol looked down from the boardroom; Taylor looked up from the shop floor. Same goal of better management, very different lenses.
points: Perspective: Fayol from top management; Taylor from the supervisory (shop floor) level.
Unity of command: Fayol was a staunch supporter; Taylor did not consider it important (functional foremanship gives eight bosses).
Applicability: Fayol's principles are universally applicable; Taylor's apply to specialised situations.
Basis of formation: Fayol used personal experience; Taylor used observation and experimentation.

Focus: Fayol on improving overall administration; Taylor on increasing productivity. Personality: Fayol a practitioner; Taylor a scientist. Expression: Fayol's general theory of administration; Taylor's scientific management.

example.q: In a case, workers at Sunshine Bottling were timed, given rest breaks and paid more for exceeding the standard. Name the techniques and the thinker.
steps: Timing workers = time study
Rest breaks = fatigue study
Higher pay above standard = differential piece wage system
All three are Taylor's techniques of scientific management

learn.hook: A sudden RBI rate hike, a viral health trend, a new law on plastic: none is in a company's control, yet each can make or break its year.
points: Business environment is the total of all individuals, institutions and other forces that are outside the control of a business enterprise but may affect its performance.

Totality of external forces: it is the sum of everything outside the firm. Specific and general forces: specific forces (investors, customers, competitors, suppliers) affect a firm directly; general forces (economic, social, political, legal, technological) affect all firms indirectly.
Inter-relatedness: the forces are linked, e.g. a health trend raises demand for organic food, which brings new firms and new rules. Dynamic nature: the environment keeps changing.
Uncertainty: future changes are hard to predict, especially in fast-moving fields like IT and fashion. Complexity: many forces act together, making their combined effect hard to understand.
Relativity: the impact differs from country to country and region to region, e.g. demand for a product may be high in one region and low in another.

example.q: Saree demand is huge in parts of India but small in many other countries. Which feature of business environment does this show?
steps: The same product faces different conditions in different places.
So the environment's effect depends on the local context.
This is the relativity of business environment.

learn.reallife: When the government cut GST rates on some products, demand rose, competitors cut prices and suppliers raised output: a neat picture of inter-related environmental forces.

learn.hook: The first company to spot India's demand for small, fuel-efficient cars in the 1980s ruled the market for decades. Reading the environment early pays!
points: Enables the firm to identify opportunities and get the first-mover advantage: being early to spot a trend lets a firm lead the market.
Helps identify threats and early warning signals: e.g. news of a strong foreign competitor entering lets a firm prepare.
Helps in tapping useful resources: the environment is the source of finance, machines, raw material and people.
Helps in coping with rapid changes: firms aware of changes can respond quickly. Assists in planning and policy formulation.
Helps in improving performance: firms that continuously monitor the environment perform better.

example.q: Swastik Tea learns that a global brand will enter India next year. It improves its packaging and widens distribution in advance. Which importance is shown?
steps: The news of the new entrant is a threat.
Learning about it early is an early warning signal.
Preparing in advance shows identifying threats and early warning signals.
example.answer: Identification of threats and early warning signals

learn.reallife: When digital payments grew after 2016, fintech startups that spotted the opportunity early won a first-mover advantage in UPI apps.

learn.hook: A festive season boom, a jump in loan interest rates and a new phone that kills the old one: three different dimensions of the same environment.
points: Economic environment: interest rates, inflation, change in people's disposable income, stock market indices and the value of the rupee. E.g. a rise in interest rates makes borrowing costlier for firms and buyers.

Social environment: customs, traditions, values, social trends and society's expectations from business. E.g. festivals like Diwali, Eid and Christmas raise demand; health trends raise demand for organic food; more women working raises demand for ready-to-cook food and creches.

Technological environment: scientific improvements and innovations that offer new ways of producing goods and services and new methods of running a business. E.g. digital watches hurt traditional watchmakers; online platforms changed retail.

example.q: Classify: (i) the rupee falls against the US dollar; (ii) urban families prefer smaller pack sizes; (iii) UPI replaces cheques for small payments.
steps: (i) Value of rupee = economic
(ii) Changing lifestyle and social trend = social
(iii) New method of payment through innovation = technological

topics.title: Dimensions: political and legal, and identifying dimensions

learn.hook: Investors love a stable country, and tobacco ads must carry a health warning by law. Politics and law shape business too.
points: Political environment: political conditions such as general stability and peace in the country and the specific attitudes of elected government representatives towards business. Stability builds investor confidence.

Legal environment: legislation passed by Parliament, administrative orders issued by government authorities, court judgements and decisions of commissions and agencies. E.g. laws require a statutory health warning on cigarette packs, and advertising of alcoholic drinks is prohibited.

Identifying the dimension: ask what caused the change. Money or prices = economic; habits and values = social; new methods or products = technological; government stability or attitude = political; laws, courts or regulations = legal.

example.q: A court orders that all food delivery packaging must be compostable within a year. Which dimension, and what should food firms do?
steps: A court judgement changes the rules for business.

Firms must plan to switch packaging in time to comply.

learn.hook: On the night of 8 November 2016, ₹500 and ₹1000 notes ceased to be legal tender. Queues at banks, a rush to digital wallets, and a big lesson in business environment!
points: Demonetisation: the Government of India announced on 8 November 2016 that ₹500 and ₹1000 notes would no longer be legal tender. New ₹500 and ₹2000 notes were issued.

It was a tax administration measure: people holding old notes had to deposit them in banks, bringing hidden cash into the tax net. Those with unaccounted cash had to declare it and pay tax or face scrutiny.
It aimed to curb corruption, counterfeit currency, terrorism financing and black money.
It aimed to channelise savings into the formal financial system, as cash was deposited in banks.
It aimed to create a less-cash (cash-lite) economy by pushing digital payments, leading to more formalisation of the economy.

example.q: After demonetisation, Raju's tea stall started accepting payments through a QR code. Which feature of demonetisation does this reflect?
steps: Cash became scarce for a while.
People and businesses moved to digital modes.
This reflects the aim of creating a less-cash economy.
example.answer: Creating a less-cash economy through digital payments

learn.reallife: Small shops across India began displaying UPI and wallet QR codes widely after 2016, showing how a policy change in the economic environment reshaped everyday business.

learn.hook: Before a single brick of a metro line is laid, engineers have planned routes, budgets and timelines for years. Planning is thinking before doing.
points: Planning is deciding in advance what to do and how to do it. It bridges the gap between where we are and where we want to go.
Planning focuses on achieving objectives and is the primary function of management: it lays the base for all other functions.
Planning is pervasive (needed at all levels and in all departments, with different scope) and continuous (a plan is made for a period, then a new plan follows).

Planning is futuristic (it looks ahead and forecasts the future), involves decision making (choosing among alternatives) and is a mental exercise (it needs foresight, imagination and sound judgement).

example.q: Top management at Vega Motors plans a 5-year expansion, while a supervisor plans the next day's shift schedule. Which feature of planning is shown?
steps: Planning happens at the top and at the supervisory level.

learn.hook: A cricket team that has planned its bowling changes doesn't panic when the opponent smashes 20 in an over. Plans calm the chaos.
points: Provides direction: it tells employees in advance what to do and how.

Reduces overlapping and wasteful activities: plans coordinate the activities of departments and people.
Promotes innovative ideas: planning is the first function and lets managers think of new ideas.
Facilitates decision making: managers choose the best among alternatives. Establishes standards for controlling: plans give the standards against which actual performance is measured.

learn.hook: Some firms make a perfect 5-year plan, then a pandemic arrives in year one. Plans have limits too.
points: Leads to rigidity: managers may feel they must stick to the plan even when circumstances change.
May not work in a dynamic environment: the environment keeps changing, and plans cannot foresee every change.
Reduces creativity: if middle and lower managers only follow plans made by top management, they get little chance to use initiative.
Involves huge costs: time and money are spent on research, experts and discussions, which may not always justify the benefits.
Is a time-consuming process: there may be little time left for action. Does not guarantee success: a good plan must still be implemented well; success also depends on execution.

example.q: Rohan Retail spent 6 months and ₹10 lakh on a market study before opening a store, by which time a rival had already opened in the same area. Which limitations are shown?
steps: The study took 6 months, leaving no time to act first.
It also cost a large sum.
This shows planning is time-consuming and involves huge costs.

learn.reallife: Several firms with rigid annual plans struggled when lockdowns hit in 2020, while those with flexible plans pivoted faster. Planning can lead to rigidity.

learn.hook: A family planning a wedding sets a budget, assumes the guest count, lists venue options, compares them, picks one, books it and keeps checking. That is the planning process!
points: Step 1 Setting objectives: decide what the organisation wants to achieve; objectives flow down to departments.
Step 2 Developing premises: assumptions about the future, e.g. forecasts of demand, interest rates, government policy. All managers should use the same premises.
Step 3 Identifying alternative courses of action. Step 4 Evaluating alternative courses: weigh positive and negative aspects of each in light of objectives.
Step 5 Selecting an alternative: choose the best (most feasible, profitable, with fewest negative consequences), sometimes a combination.
Step 6 Implementing the plan: putting it into action. Step 7 Follow-up action: monitoring whether the plan is being implemented as intended.

example.q: Uday Agro assumes the monsoon will be normal and fertiliser demand will rise 10% next year. Which step of planning is this?
steps: These are assumptions about future conditions.
Assumptions that underlie plans are called premises.
So this is developing premises (step 2).

learn.reallife: Before launching a new train service, railways estimate passenger demand (premises), compare route options (alternatives), choose one, start operations and keep monitoring occupancy (follow-up).

topics.title: Types of plans: single-use, standing, objectives, strategy, policy

learn.hook: A company's 'no credit beyond 30 days' policy is used for years, but its Diwali sale plan is used just once. Plans come in different shapes.
points: Single-use plans are made for a one-time event or project that is unlikely to be repeated, e.g. budgets, programmes and projects. Standing plans are used repeatedly for recurring situations, e.g. policies, procedures, methods and rules.

Objectives are the end results which management wants to achieve. They should be expressed in specific terms, be measurable, have a time limit and be stated in quantitative terms where possible, e.g. 'raise sales by 10% in a year'.

Strategy is a comprehensive plan for accomplishing an organisation's objectives. It covers: determining long-term objectives, adopting a particular course of action and allocating resources. It takes the business environment into account.
Policies are general statements that guide thinking or channel energies towards a particular direction, e.g. a recruitment policy or a pricing policy. They leave room for managerial discretion.

example.q: Classify: (i) 'We aim to achieve a 20% market share by 2028.' (ii) 'We will enter rural markets with low-priced sachets, backed by a ₹50 crore budget.' (iii) 'We recruit only graduates for sales posts.'
steps: (i) A specific, measurable end result = objective
(ii) A comprehensive course of action with resource allocation = strategy
(iii) A general statement that guides decisions = policy

learn.reallife: When an Indian phone maker decides to fight a global rival with low prices, online-only sales and heavy local marketing, it is framing a strategy.

topics.title: Procedures, methods, rules, programmes and budgets

learn.hook: 'No mobile phones on the shop floor' leaves no choice. 'Steps to claim travel expenses' leaves no doubt. Different plans, different jobs!
points: Procedure: routine steps on how to carry out an activity, in chronological order. It is meant for internal use, e.g. the procedure for granting leave.

Method: the prescribed way or manner in which a task has to be performed, given the objective, e.g. on-the-job or off-the-job training methods. Procedure is a series of steps for an activity; method is the way of doing one step or task.

Rule: a specific statement telling what is to be done or not done. No flexibility or discretion; violation may lead to a penalty, e.g. 'No smoking in the factory'. A policy is a general guide with discretion; a rule is rigid.
Programme: a detailed statement about a project, outlining objectives, policies, procedures, rules, tasks, resources and timing. It combines several plans for a one-time project.
Budget: a statement of expected results expressed in numerical terms, e.g. a sales budget for the year. It is a planning device and also a control device.

example.q: Classify: (i) 'Wearing a helmet in the plant is compulsory.' (ii) 'Fill form, get it signed by the HOD, submit to accounts.' (iii) 'Sales next year: ₹40 crore.'
steps: (i) A specific must-do with no discretion = rule
(ii) Chronological steps = procedure
(iii) Expected results in numbers = budget

learn.hook: A plan to run a hospital is just paper until someone decides who does surgery, who runs the pharmacy and who reports to whom. That is organising.
points: Organising is the process of identifying and grouping the work to be performed, defining and delegating responsibility and authority, and establishing relationships so that people can work together to achieve objectives.
Step 1 Identification and division of work: the total work is divided into manageable activities as per plans, avoiding duplication.
Step 2 Departmentalisation: similar activities are grouped into departments, units or sections, e.g. by function (production, finance) or by product or territory.
Step 3 Assignment of duties: jobs are allocated to members of each department according to their skills (the right person for the right job).
Step 4 Establishing reporting relationships: each person knows from whom to take orders and to whom to report, creating a hierarchy.

example.q: A new school's principal lists all tasks, forms academic, sports and admin wings, gives each teacher duties, and decides that wing heads report to her. Name the steps in order.
steps: Listing all tasks = identification and division of work
Forming wings = departmentalisation
Giving teachers duties = assignment of duties
Wing heads report to principal = establishing reporting relationships
example.answer: Division of work, departmentalisation, assignment of duties, reporting relationships

topics.title: Organisation structure, span of management and functional structure

learn.hook: If one manager can handle 8 people well, how many managers does a team of 64 need? The answer shapes the whole organisation chart.
points: Organisation structure is the framework within which managerial and operating tasks are performed. It specifies relationships between people, work and resources.

Span of management is the number of subordinates that can be effectively managed by a superior. It determines the levels of management: a narrow span gives more levels (a tall structure) and a wide span gives fewer levels (a flat structure).
Functional structure groups jobs of a similar nature by function, e.g. production, purchase, marketing, finance, HR, each under a head reporting to the top.
Suitable when the organisation is large, has diversified activities and operations need a high degree of specialisation.

Advantages: occupational specialisation, better control and coordination within a department, managerial efficiency, minimal duplication (economies of scale), easier training, attention to all functional areas. Disadvantages: less emphasis on overall objectives (functional empires), coordination problems across departments, conflicts of interest, and inflexibility (narrow perspective).

example.q: A firm has 48 workers. If each supervisor can handle 6 workers and each manager can handle 4 supervisors, how many supervisors and managers are needed?
steps: Supervisors = 48 ÷ 6 = 8
Managers = 8 ÷ 4 = 2
So 8 supervisors and 2 managers (a wider span would need fewer of both)

topics.title: Divisional structure and comparison with functional

learn.hook: A company that makes cosmetics, edible oils and steel tubes can't run them all from one marketing department. Enter the divisional structure.
points: Divisional structure groups activities by product lines (or regions); each division is a separate unit with its own functions (production, marketing, finance) and a divisional manager responsible for profit or loss.
Suitable for firms that make a large variety of products using different productive resources, or for firms that are growing and diversifying.

Advantages: product specialisation develops varied skills in divisional heads and prepares them for higher posts; each division's profit or loss can be measured, which fixes accountability; quick decisions due to autonomy; easy expansion by adding new divisions.

Disadvantages: conflict among divisional heads over funds and resources; higher costs due to duplication of activities across divisions; divisional managers may put their own division's interest above the organisation's.

Comparison: functional is based on functions, divisional on products; functional gives functional specialisation, divisional gives product specialisation; responsibility is hard to fix in functional, easy in divisional; functional has low cost (no duplication), divisional has high cost (duplication); divisional heads get wider training for top jobs; coordination across functions is harder in functional and easier within a divisional unit.

example.q: Prakriti Ltd makes soaps, juices and cricket bats. Should it use functional or divisional structure? Give one advantage.
steps: The products are very different and need different resources.
So each product should have its own unit with its own functions.
Advantage: the profit of each product division can be measured and its head held responsible.
example.answer: Divisional structure; it allows clear accountability for each product's performance

learn.reallife: Large Indian conglomerates often have separate divisions for consumer goods, hotels, paper and agri-business, each run by its own head.

learn.hook: The org chart says who reports to whom. The lunch table says who actually talks to whom. Both shape how work gets done.
points: Formal organisation: the structure deliberately designed by management, with clearly defined authority, responsibility and relationships. Features: specifies relationships, is a means to achieve objectives, coordinates efforts, is designed by top management, places emphasis on work and rules.

Advantages of formal: easy to fix responsibility, no overlapping, unity of command, easier achievement of goals and stability. Disadvantages: delays due to the scalar chain, ignores social needs (human relationships), and may not recognise creativity and talent.

Informal organisation: a network of social relationships that emerges spontaneously from interaction among employees. Features: originates within the formal organisation, behaviour is shaped by group norms, communication has no fixed direction (grapevine), has no definite structure.

Advantages of informal: faster spread of information and quick feedback, fulfils social needs and sense of belonging, compensates for gaps in the formal structure. Disadvantages: spreads rumours, may resist change, pressure to conform to group norms.

Comparison: formal arises from rules and is deliberately created; informal arises from social interaction and emerges on its own. Formal authority comes from position; informal from personal qualities. Formal follows the scalar chain and is rigid; informal has no fixed path and is flexible. Formal leaders are managers; informal leaders are chosen by the group.

steps: The group formed on its own through a shared interest.

This is informal organisation; a risk is that rumours or distorted news may spread.
example.answer: Informal organisation; it may spread rumours

learn.hook: A manager who tries to do everything herself burns out. A manager who hands over work but stays answerable for results grows a team. That is delegation.
points: Delegation is the downward transfer of authority from a superior to a subordinate. The manager remains accountable for the final outcome.
Authority: the right of an individual to command subordinates and act within the scope of the position. It arises from formal position and flows downward. It can be delegated.
Responsibility: the obligation of a subordinate to properly perform the assigned duty. It arises from the superior-subordinate relationship and flows upward. It cannot be entirely delegated.
Accountability: answerability for the final outcome. It arises from responsibility, flows upward and cannot be delegated at all. Authority should match responsibility.
Importance: effective management (managers focus on important work), employee development, motivation of employees, facilitation of growth, basis of management hierarchy, and better coordination.

example.q: Sales head Meera gives her deputy authority to approve discounts up to 5%. A wrong discount causes a loss. Who answers to the CEO?
steps: Meera delegated authority, so the deputy is responsible to Meera.

So Meera remains accountable to the CEO for the outcome.
example.answer: Meera remains accountable to the CEO

learn.hook: A pizza chain lets each outlet manager decide local offers and staffing on the spot. Head office keeps only big decisions. That is decentralisation.
points: Decentralisation means delegating decision-making authority systematically to the lowest levels, except that which can be exercised only at central points.
Centralisation keeps decision making with a few at the top. No organisation is fully centralised or fully decentralised: a balance is needed, and it shifts as the firm grows.

Importance: develops initiative among subordinates; develops managerial talent for the future; quick decision making; relief to top management; facilitates growth; better control (performance of each level can be evaluated).

Delegation vs decentralisation: delegation is a compulsory act (no manager can do everything) while decentralisation is an optional policy decision of top management. Delegation keeps more control with the superior; decentralisation gives more freedom. Delegation's scope is narrow (superior and immediate subordinate); decentralisation's scope is wide (extends to the lowest level).
Purpose: delegation reduces the burden on the manager; decentralisation increases the role of subordinates by giving them more autonomy.

example.q: Swift Couriers lets each branch head decide hiring, local pricing and vendor contracts, while the board decides only on new cities. Is this delegation or decentralisation? Give one benefit.
steps: Authority is spread systematically to the lowest levels across the whole firm.
It is a policy decision by top management.
So it is decentralisation; one benefit is quick decision making at branches.
example.answer: Decentralisation; quicker decisions at the branch level

learn.hook: A startup with a brilliant idea but the wrong team usually fails. Getting and keeping the right people is the job of staffing.
points: Staffing is filling and keeping filled the positions in the organisation structure. It puts the right person in the right job.

Importance: discovers and obtains competent personnel; ensures higher performance by placing the right person on the right job; ensures continuous survival and growth through succession planning; ensures optimum utilisation of human resources (avoids overmanning and shortage); improves job satisfaction and morale through fair rewards.

Human resource management (HRM) includes specialised activities such as recruitment, job analysis, developing compensation and incentive plans, training and development, maintaining labour relations, handling grievances, providing social security and welfare, and defending the company in lawsuits.
Evolution: from labour welfare officers (trade union era) to personnel management to modern HRM, which treats people as a valuable resource.
Staffing is both a managerial function (every manager performs it) and a part of HRM. Its aspects are recruitment, selection and training.

learn.hook: From 'how many people do we need?' to 'what should we pay them?', staffing is a chain of eight linked steps.
points: Step 1 Estimating manpower requirements: workload analysis finds the number and types of people needed; workforce analysis finds the number and types available. The gap shows over- or under-staffing.
Step 2 Recruitment: searching for prospective employees and stimulating them to apply. Step 3 Selection: choosing the best from the pool of applicants.

Step 4 Placement and orientation: placement means the employee occupying the post for which selected; orientation means introducing the employee to colleagues and familiarising them with rules and policies.
Step 5 Training and development: improving skills and preparing for growth. Step 6 Performance appraisal: evaluating actual performance against standards.

Step 7 Promotion and career planning: moving to higher positions with more responsibility. Step 8 Compensation: all forms of pay or rewards, direct (wages, salaries, incentives) and indirect (paid leave, insurance).

example.q: A new accountant at Vedant Ltd is shown her desk, introduced to the team and told about leave rules on her first day. Which step is this?
steps: She has joined the post she was selected for: placement.
She is being introduced and familiarised with rules.
This is placement and orientation.

learn.hook: Before looking outside, a smart company asks: 'Is the right person already sitting in our office?'
points: Recruitment is the process of searching for prospective employees and stimulating them to apply for jobs in the organisation. It is a positive process.

Internal sources: transfers (shifting an employee from one job to another, usually at the same level, without substantial change in responsibility or status) and promotions (shifting to a higher position with more responsibility, status and pay).

Merits: motivates employees (promotion prospects); simplifies selection and placement (candidates are already known); transfer is a training tool and helps adjust surplus or shortage of staff between departments; cheaper than external recruitment.

Limitations: no scope for fresh talent; employees may become lethargic if promotion is assured by seniority; a new enterprise cannot use internal sources; spirit of competition among employees may be hampered; frequent transfers may reduce productivity.

example.q: Agile Bank has a surplus of clerks in Pune and a shortage in Nashik. What should it do and what is the merit?
steps: Shifting staff between branches at the same level is a transfer.
Transfer is an internal source of recruitment.
Merit: it adjusts surplus and shortage of staff without hiring from outside.
example.answer: Transfer staff to Nashik; it adjusts surplus and shortage cheaply

learn.hook: From a notice at the factory gate to a job post on a website seen by millions, external recruitment has many doors.
points: Direct recruitment: a notice is placed on the notice board for vacancies; job seekers assemble at the premises. Used for casual or unskilled jobs. Casual callers: a database of unsolicited applications kept in the office.
Advertisement in newspapers and journals: wider choice but may bring a flood of applications. Employment exchanges: government-run, mainly for unskilled and skilled operative jobs.

Placement agencies and management consultants: provide a database of qualified candidates for technical, professional and managerial posts, for a fee. Campus recruitment: firms visit colleges and institutes to hire students.

Recommendations of employees: present employees suggest known people (background known, but risk of favouritism). Labour contractors: supply unskilled workers at short notice. Web publishing: job sites and company websites.
Merits of external sources: qualified personnel, wider choice, fresh talent, competitive spirit among existing staff. Limitations: dissatisfaction among existing employees, lengthy process, costly.

learn.hook: A thousand applicants, ten vacancies. Selection is the art of saying 'no' to 990 people fairly.
points: Selection is the process of identifying and choosing the best person out of the pool of applicants. It is called a negative process because it rejects more candidates than it accepts.
Steps: preliminary screening, selection tests, employment interview, reference and background checks, selection decision, medical examination, job offer and contract of employment.

Tests: intelligence test (mental ability, IQ, reasoning), aptitude test (potential to learn new skills), personality test (emotions, maturity, value system), trade test (existing skills and knowledge for the job) and interest test (pattern of interests).

Recruitment vs selection: recruitment attracts candidates (positive), selection chooses the best (negative). Recruitment comes first; selection follows. Recruitment is simple; selection is complex and lengthy.

learn.hook: A bank teaches a new clerk to use its software: training. It sends a branch manager on a leadership course: development. Same goal of growth, different focus.
points: Training: increasing the knowledge and skills of an employee for doing a particular job. It is job-oriented.

Development: growth of an individual in all respects, including personality, maturity and potential. It is career-oriented. Education: increasing the knowledge and understanding of employees in a broader, conceptual sense.

Benefits to the organisation: systematic learning reduces wastage of effort and money; higher productivity; prepares future managers; increased morale and lower absenteeism and turnover; effective response to the changing environment.
Benefits to employees: better career opportunities, higher earnings, fewer accidents (better handling of machines), increased satisfaction and morale.
Induction training helps a new employee settle down quickly by becoming familiar with the people, surroundings, job and business.

example.q: Is this training or development? (i) Teaching a cashier to use a new billing system. (ii) A mentoring programme to build a manager's leadership and decision skills.

learn.hook: Learning to fly a plane? You'd better start in a simulator, not the real cockpit. Choosing the right training method matters.
points: On-the-job methods (learning while doing): apprenticeship programmes (trainee works under a master worker for a long period, for trades like plumbing and electrical work), coaching (superior guides the trainee as a coach, often to prepare a successor), internship training (joint programme of educational institutions and firms, combining theory and practice) and job rotation (shifting the trainee from one department to another).
Off-the-job methods (learning away from the work place): classroom lectures and conferences, films, case study, computer modelling, vestibule training and programmed instruction.
Vestibule training: employees learn on equipment similar to the actual machines in a separate area (a dummy model). Used when equipment is costly or sophisticated, to avoid damage and accidents.
Programmed instruction: information is broken into small, logical units; the learner answers and gets feedback (rewards) at each step. Computer modelling simulates the work environment.

example.q: A new airline pilot practises emergency landings in a flight simulator. Which method is this, and why is it used?
steps: The trainee uses equipment like the real one, but away from the actual job.

This is vestibule training (with computer modelling), an off-the-job method.

learn.hook: Plans are ready, teams are formed, people are hired. But nothing moves until someone says 'Let's go!' Directing is the spark that starts the engine.
points: Directing means instructing, guiding, communicating with and inspiring people in the organisation to achieve its objectives.
Characteristics: directing initiates action; takes place at every level of management (pervasive); is a continuous process; and flows from top to bottom (a manager directs subordinates).

Importance: initiates action; integrates employees' efforts towards common goals; is a means of motivation; facilitates implementation of changes (by reducing resistance through communication and motivation); and brings stability and balance in the organisation.
Elements of directing: supervision, motivation, leadership and communication.

example.q: When Nirmal Foods decided to shift to automated packing, its managers explained the benefits, trained workers and assured job security, so the change went smoothly. Which importance of directing is shown?

learn.hook: A supervisor in a garment unit settles a quarrel, teaches a new stitch and passes a worker's idea to the manager, all before lunch. That is supervision.
points: Principles of directing: maximum individual contribution; harmony of objectives (individual and organisational goals should match); unity of command; appropriateness of direction technique (suited to subordinates' needs and abilities); managerial communication (clear, and understood as intended); use of informal organisation; leadership; and follow-through (checking whether instructions are being implemented).
Supervision means overseeing subordinates at work. Its meaning varies with the level, but it is especially important at the first line (supervisory) level.

Role or importance of a supervisor: maintains day-to-day contact and friendly relations with workers; acts as a link between workers and management (link pin); maintains group unity by settling disputes; ensures work is done as per targets; provides on-the-job training; builds positive attitudes through leadership; and analyses work and gives feedback.

topics.title: Motivation: meaning, features, process and importance

learn.hook: Why does one salesperson make 50 calls a day and another only 10, with the same salary? The answer is motivation.
points: Motive: an inner state that energises, activates or moves and directs behaviour towards goals. Motivation: the process of stimulating people to action to accomplish desired goals. Motivators: the techniques used to motivate people, e.g. pay, bonus, promotion, recognition.

Features: motivation is an internal feeling; it produces goal-directed behaviour; it can be positive (rewards, promotion) or negative (punishment, stopping increments); it is a complex process because people differ in needs and reactions.
Process: unsatisfied need → tension → drives → search behaviour → satisfied need → reduction of tension.
Importance: improves performance; changes negative or indifferent attitudes to positive ones; reduces employee turnover; reduces absenteeism; helps introduce changes smoothly.

example.q: Neha wants a promotion. She feels restless, so she joins an evening course and takes on extra projects. After she is promoted, she feels at ease. Map this to the motivation process.
steps: Unsatisfied need: promotion

Satisfied need: promotion achieved
Reduction of tension: she feels at ease

learn.hook: First you need food, then a safe room, then friends, then respect, and finally the chance to become your best self. Maslow arranged our needs like a staircase.
points: Abraham Maslow's need hierarchy has five levels, from lowest to highest: physiological, safety or security, affiliation or belonging (social), esteem, and self-actualisation.

Physiological needs: basic survival needs like food, water, shelter and sleep; met through basic salary. Safety needs: physical and economic security, e.g. job security, stability of income, pension plans.
Affiliation or belonging needs: affection, sense of belonging, acceptance and friendship. Esteem needs: self-respect, autonomy, status, recognition and attention.
Self-actualisation: the highest need, to become what one is capable of becoming, including growth, self-fulfilment and achievement of goals.
Assumptions: behaviour depends on needs; needs are in a hierarchical order; a satisfied need no longer motivates; a person moves to the next higher level only when the lower need is satisfied.

example.q: Identify the need: (i) Ravi wants a permanent job with a pension. (ii) Priya wants to be named 'Best Designer' at the annual meet. (iii) Arjun wants to start his own research lab to fulfil his potential.
steps: (i) Job security and pension = safety needs
(ii) Recognition and status = esteem needs
(iii) Reaching one's full potential = self-actualisation

learn.hook: Money talks, but so does a thank-you, a challenging project and a say in decisions. Smart firms use both kinds of incentives.
points: Financial incentives are direct or indirect monetary rewards: pay and allowances (salary, dearness allowance, increments); productivity-linked wage incentives; bonus (over and above wages); profit sharing; co-partnership or stock option (shares offered to employees at a price lower than the market price); retirement benefits (provident fund, pension, gratuity); perquisites (car, housing, medical aid, children's education).

Non-financial incentives satisfy psychological, social and emotional needs: status (rank of positions); organisational climate (e.g. autonomy, rewarding orientation, concern for employees); career advancement opportunity; job enrichment (more variety, higher knowledge and skills, more autonomy and responsibility in the job); employee recognition programmes; job security; employee participation (e.g. joint management committees, work committees, canteen committees, suggestion programmes); and employee empowerment (more autonomy and powers to subordinates).
Financial incentives mainly satisfy lower-level needs; non-financial incentives mainly satisfy higher-level needs like esteem and self-actualisation.

learn.hook: One captain barks orders, another discusses field placements, a third lets senior players decide. Three different leadership styles, and each can work in the right setting.
points: Leadership is the process of influencing the behaviour of people by making them strive voluntarily towards achieving organisational goals.

Features: it is an ability to influence others; it tries to bring change in people's behaviour; it shows the interpersonal relation between leader and followers; it is exercised to achieve common goals; it is a continuous process.
Importance: influences behaviour; maintains personal relations and helps followers meet their needs; introduces required changes; handles conflicts; prepares successors through training.

Styles based on use of authority: autocratic or authoritarian (gives orders and expects compliance; decisions centralised; one-way communication; useful for quick decisions or when subordinates need close supervision); democratic or participative (decides in consultation with subordinates; two-way communication; encourages participation); laissez-faire or free-rein (gives subordinates high independence; leader mainly supports; suits competent and responsible subordinates).

example.q: Identify the style: (i) Captain Rana decides every field placement himself and allows no discussion. (ii) Manager Sana asks her team for ideas before finalising a plan. (iii) Professor Iyer lets her expert researchers set their own goals and methods.
steps: (i) Orders with no consultation = autocratic
(ii) Consultation and participation = democratic
(iii) High independence to experts = laissez-faire

learn.hook: A manager sends a WhatsApp message: 'Meet at 5.' Half the team comes at 5 a.m. Communication is not just sending; it is being understood.
points: Communication is the process of exchange of ideas, views, facts and feelings between two or more persons to create a common understanding.

Elements: sender (conveys the message), message (content of ideas or feelings), encoding (converting the message into words, symbols or gestures), media (the path: face-to-face, phone, email, letter), decoding (converting the symbols back into meaning), receiver (who gets the message), feedback (receiver's response showing the message was understood) and noise (any obstruction or hindrance, e.g. poor phone line, inattention, ambiguous symbols).

Importance: basis of coordination; helps smooth working of the enterprise; basis of decision making; increases managerial efficiency; promotes cooperation and industrial peace; establishes effective leadership; boosts morale and provides motivation.

Decoding: the team reading and understanding the words
Feedback: the reply 'Noted, will do'

learn.hook: The official circular says the office will shift next month. But everyone already knew from the lunch-time grapevine last week!
points: Formal communication follows the official chain of command. Vertical: downward (superior to subordinate, e.g. orders, notices, circulars) and upward (subordinate to superior, e.g. leave applications, grievances, suggestions). Horizontal or lateral: between people at the same level in different departments, e.g. production manager and marketing manager.

Formal networks: single chain (from a superior to a subordinate through a chain, one link at a time), wheel (all subordinates communicate through one superior at the centre), circular (each person communicates with neighbours; slow), free flow (everyone communicates with everyone; fast) and inverted V (a subordinate may communicate with the immediate superior and also with the superior's superior, in a limited way).

Informal communication (grapevine) arises from social interaction, without following official channels. Grapevine networks: single strand (each person tells one other in a sequence), gossip (one person tells everyone non-selectively), probability (a person tells others at random) and cluster (a person tells only those he or she trusts).

Formal vs informal: formal follows the scalar chain, is slower, keeps records and is official; informal follows no fixed path, spreads fast, may distort information and has no records. Managers can use the grapevine to spread useful information and get feedback.

example.q: At Bloom Ltd, every regional manager reports to and receives instructions from the national sales head only; they don't talk to each other. Which network is this?
steps: All communication passes through one central person.
The others do not communicate directly with each other.

learn.hook: The boss says 'This report is quite good.' One worker hears praise, another hears criticism. Somewhere a barrier is hiding.
points: Semantic barriers (problems in encoding and decoding): badly expressed message; symbols or words with different meanings (e.g. 'value' can mean price, worth or importance); faulty translations; unclarified assumptions; technical jargon; misreading body language and gestures.

Psychological or emotional barriers: premature evaluation (judging before hearing fully); lack of attention; loss by transmission and poor retention (information is lost as it passes through many people); distrust between sender and receiver.

Organisational barriers: organisational policy (if it does not support free flow); rules and regulations (rigid, time-consuming routes); status (status-conscious managers keep distance); complexity in organisation structure (more levels cause delay and distortion); lack of organisational facilities (meetings, suggestion boxes, open-door policy).

Personal barriers: fear of challenge to authority (a superior withholds information); lack of confidence of the superior in subordinates; unwillingness to communicate (subordinates fear it may hurt them); lack of proper incentives for communication.

learn.hook: A car's dashboard tells the driver if speed, fuel or engine heat drifts from normal. Controlling is a manager's dashboard.
points: Controlling means ensuring that activities in an organisation are performed as per the plans. It involves comparing actual performance with standards and taking corrective action.
It is a goal-oriented and pervasive function (needed at all levels and in all organisations).
Controlling is both backward-looking (it checks past performance, like a post-mortem) and forward-looking (it improves future performance by correcting deviations).

Importance: accomplishing organisational goals; judging the accuracy of standards; making efficient use of resources; improving employee motivation (employees know in advance on what basis they will be judged); ensuring order and discipline; facilitating coordination in action (all departments work to predetermined standards).
